<para id="import-auto-id1411966"><term id="import-auto-id2593990">Radioactive dating</term> is a clever use of naturally occurring radioactivity. Its most famous application is <term id="import-auto-id2604011">carbon-14 dating</term>. Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years and is produced in a nuclear reaction induced when neutrons produced by cosmic rays strike <m:math xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mmultiscripts><m:mn>N</m:mn><m:mprescripts /><m:none /><m:mtext>14</m:mtext></m:mmultiscripts></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{"" lSup { size 8{"14"} } N} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> in the atmosphere. Radioactive carbon has the same chemistry as stable carbon, and so it mixes into the ecosphere, where it is consumed and becomes part of every living organism. Carbon-14 has an abundance of 1.3 parts per trillion of normal carbon. Thus, if you know the number of carbon nuclei in an object (perhaps determined by mass and Avogadro’s number), you multiply that number by <m:math xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mn>1.3</m:mn><m:mo>×</m:mo><m:msup><m:mn>10</m:mn><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mo stretchy="false">−</m:mo><m:mn>12</m:mn></m:mrow></m:mrow></m:msup></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow></m:semantics></m:math> to find the number of 
<m:math xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mmultiscripts><m:mtext>C</m:mtext><m:mprescripts /><m:none /><m:mtext>14</m:mtext></m:mmultiscripts></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow></m:semantics></m:math> nuclei in the object. When an organism dies, carbon exchange with the environment ceases, and 
<m:math xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mmultiscripts><m:mtext>C</m:mtext><m:mprescripts /><m:none /><m:mtext>14</m:mtext></m:mmultiscripts></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow></m:semantics></m:math> is not replenished as it decays. By comparing the abundance of 
<m:math xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mmultiscripts><m:mtext>C</m:mtext><m:mprescripts /><m:none /><m:mtext>14</m:mtext></m:mmultiscripts></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow></m:semantics></m:math> in an artifact, such as mummy wrappings, with the normal abundance in living tissue, it is possible to determine the artifact’s age (or time since death). Carbon-14 dating can be used for biological tissues as old as 50 or 60 thousand years, but is most accurate for younger samples, since the abundance of 
<m:math xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mmultiscripts><m:mtext>C</m:mtext><m:mprescripts /><m:none /><m:mtext>14</m:mtext></m:mmultiscripts></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow></m:semantics></m:math> nuclei in them is greater. Very old biological materials contain no 
<m:math xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mmultiscripts><m:mtext>C</m:mtext><m:mprescripts /><m:none /><m:mtext>14</m:mtext></m:mmultiscripts></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow></m:semantics></m:math> at all. There are instances in which the date of an artifact can be determined by other means, such as historical knowledge or tree-ring counting. These cross-references have confirmed the validity of carbon-14 dating and permitted us to calibrate the technique as well. Carbon-14 dating revolutionized parts of archaeology and is of such importance that it earned the 1960 Nobel Prize in chemistry for its developer, the American chemist Willard Libby (1908–1980).</para>
